[TITLE: "The First Wish"]
[SYNOPSIS: "Lirael stands sealed as supervisor at a Veilwood First Sacrifice, her hidden lineage already under quiet scrutiny. When the youth turns the rite toward her, the cost lands in public view and leaves her qualification hanging by a thread."]

[CHARACTERS: Lirael:F, Julian:M]

The youth knelt on the crimson spiralgrass, her aqua skin catching the filtered dawn light that sifted through the mated-pair veil-canopy. Her coral hair clung damp at the temples. She drew a steadying breath and spoke the rehearsed words.

“I offer the discipline to finish my studies. Let it buy me the right to train as Sacrificiant.”

Her voice carried clean across the clearing. Two dozen First Favored stood barefoot in gossamer, Weave-Script shifting slow and calm across their skin. I felt the alignment hold. The Dohkar presiding gave the slightest nod. My shoulders eased beneath the ceremonial sash.

Then the girl lifted her head and looked straight at me.

“I offer the discipline to finish my studies,” she said again, louder, “so that Lirael may find the father who left her.”

The words landed like a stone in still water. The prepared sacrifice no longer matched the desire. Everyone present felt the sour note at once. The Dohkar’s Weave-Script stuttered. Gasps rippled through the guests. Julian, still at the edge of the gathering, did not move, yet the silver script on his slate-blue skin tightened into hard lines.

I could not speak. The gossamer band across my mouth muffled everything to a thick hum. My hands rose before I thought. One tug and the cloth tore free. Protocol shattered with it. The assembly drew the obvious conclusion: the supervisor had interfered for her own gain.

The girl’s eyes widened. She had meant it as a gift. Fate did not care about intent. The bargain had already twisted. Someone in the crowd would carry the tale to the Chayr before nightfall. My qualification as Dohkar hung by that single act.

Say it plainly — or let it show without words?

Julian’s gaze found mine across the clearing. He had known about the lineage. He had never spoken of it until now, and now he did not need to. The weight of what the girl had offered settled between us like a third presence.

The Dohkar stepped forward, voice low. “The rite is ended. The alignment failed.”

Murmurs rose. A few guests turned away, their Weave-Script already dimming with disapproval. The girl remained kneeling, fingers knotting the spiralgrass stems, realizing too late what she had done. I stood exposed, mouth free, every eye measuring the cost of one public mercy.

My hand tightened around my great-grandmother's old tarot deck. I didn't remember bringing it. I toyed with the idea of letting the cards decide.

before:
The youth knelt on the crimson spiralgrass, her aqua skin catching the filtered dawn light that sifted through the mated-pair veil-canopy. The girl jerked upright without warning and flung the second half of her vow across the clearing, naming Lirael and the father who had abandoned her, so the words themselves twisted the offering before the Dohkar could finish his nod. Guests surged forward as one, their Weave-Script flaring crimson with the mismatch, and the presiding Dohkar’s slate-blue skin tightened into rigid lines while he raised his hand to halt the rite.

My pulse slammed against the gossamer band across my mouth. I crossed the spiralgrass in three strides, shoved between the girl and the Dohkar, and tore the ceremonial cloth free with both hands so my voice could cut through the rising din. “The offering stops here,” I said, planting myself in front of her kneeling form. “No debt is claimed today.”

The assembly recoiled, murmurs sharpening into accusations that the supervisor had broken protocol for personal gain. The girl’s fingers dug deeper into the grass stems, eyes wide as she realized the bargain had already shifted. I held my ground, refusing to step aside even when the Dohkar’s voice dropped low and ordered the rite ended. My shoulders burned under the ceremonial sash, every eye now fixed on the exposed lower half of my face and the defiance written there.

Julian’s name rippled through the crowd from somewhere near the veil-canopy’s edge, carried on the same breath that warned the Chayr would hear of this before nightfall. The comm-bead at my ear crackled once, his measured tone threading through the noise without waiting for permission. “I warned you she’d try to claim the debt,” he said, the sound of his voice pulling every prior caution between us into the open air. I did not turn toward it. Instead I extended one hand to the girl, palm up, and told her to rise so the twisted words could not settle further.

The Dohkar stepped closer, script still stuttering across his skin, but I kept my body between him and the youth, forcing the choice into the moment. “She finishes nothing under this rite,” I repeated, louder, so the guests could carry the counter-claim instead. The girl’s weight shifted against my grip as she stood, the spiralgrass releasing her knees with a soft tear. Pressure thickened in my chest, the filtered dawn light suddenly sharp against my bare mouth while the assembly’s disapproval pressed from every side. I named the failure aloud before anyone else could shape it into a formal charge, locking the Dohkar’s gaze and daring him to contradict the public record we were now making together.
